Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas · Conversation, family & daily routines

excited adjective

thrilled, full of eager joy

also be excited, thrilled, so excited, jump for joy

classical

Ter. Eun. 558: Chaerea, quid est quod sīc gestīs?
Cic. Fin. 2.14 (Lewis & Short): quōrum alter laetitiā gestiat, alter dolōre cruciētur

gestiō, gestīre, gestīvī, gestītum

verb, fourth conjugation, intransitive: absolutely, with the ablative (laetitiā gestīre) or with an infinitive

be excited, be beside oneself with joy; be itching to

Properly, to throw oneself about with joy, as a child does (Festus, in Lewis & Short); with an infinitive, to be dying to do something (see be itching to). Cicero sometimes uses it of joy out of measure.

Other words

  • exsultō, exsultāre, exsultāvī, exsultātum — jump for joy, exult

    verb, first conjugation, intransitive: with the ablative of the cause · also used · classical · Cic. Tusc. 5.16 (Lewis & Short): inānī laetitiā exsultāns et temere gestiēns; Traupman 155: exsultāre, jump for joy

    Literally to leap up, of horses and fish; of people, to leap for joy, and also to exult over someone or to boast (Lewis & Short).

  • commōtus, commōta, commōtum — stirred, worked up

    adjective: the participle of commoveō · also used · classical · Traupman 152: commōtus, excited; Traupman 311

    Traupman’s word for “excited”, but in classical Latin it is any strong stirring of the mind, and most often agitation, alarm or upset (Lewis & Short; see affect). For happy excitement say gestiō.

Examples

  • Chaerea, quid est quod sīc gestīs? quid sibi hic vestītus quaerit? Quid est quod laetus sīs?

    Chaerea, why are you so excited? What’s the meaning of these clothes? What are you so happy about?Ter. Eun. 558–559

  • ut aliquid scīre sē gaudeant? ut id aliīs narrāre gestiant?

    how glad they are to know something, and how they long to tell it to others?Cic. Fin. 5.48

See also excite, be itching to, look forward to, glad, joy.
